To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) mitochondrial glycerophhos-phate dehydrogenase is a key enzyme in the regulation of glucose metabolism in pancreatic islets; (b) the enzyme is deficient in islets from animal models of type II (non-insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus; (c) this deficiency may contribute to the impaired glucose-induced insulin release characteristic of type II diabetes.
the decreased activity of mitochondrial glycerophospha- te dehydrogenase in the islets of animals with type 2 diabetes is accompanied by a decreased content of that enzyme.
the mitochondrial glycerophosphatdehydrogenase deficiency, which has been documented in islet preparations from diabetic rats, is due to a decreased content of the enzyme.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a possible role for m-GDH in the pathogenesis of diabetes mellitus.

a new aspect of the pathogenesis of diabetes, i.e. a possible link between mitochondrial glycerophosphorylase deficiency and the development of the disease in the two experimental rat models of non-insulino-dependent diabetes mellitus.
the characterization of the pancreatic islet m-GDH deficiency in two animal species with a high susceptibility to non-insulin-dependent (type II) diabetes mellitus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

m-GDH deficiency in islet mitochondria of GK rats and neonatally STZ-treated rats is the result of a primary lesion in the islet cell, and that this lesion is the cause of non-insulin dependent diabetes mellitus in these two animal models.
the m-GDH deficiency is a primary defect in the endocrine cells of the diabetic animals.
the m-GDH is a key enzyme in glucose-induced insulin secretion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
m-GDH plays a key role in the pathogenesis of NIDDM.
the m-GDH deficiency is not a cause of diabetes, but a consequence of it.
the islets of GK rats have a decreased content of m-GDH, whereas in STZ rats both the activity and the protein content of m-GPDH are decreased.
The main takeaway from our work is that
m-GDH is a key enzyme in the regulation of glycolysis and glycogen metabolism.
the decreased m-GDH activity in islet homogentates from GK rats and STZ rats is caused by the reduced m-GDH protein content.
the decreased content of m-GDH is a feature common to two models of non-insulintype 2 diabetes, which is characterized by a relative lack of beta cell mass and a reduced insulin secretion.
